classification_signals: "This paper provides a tentative set of ideas which attempt to draw together research from neuroscience, spatial cognition and architecture (space syntax)." (p. 1)

"This paper will be presented in two sections; the first will examine three distinct and dissociated academic fields... The second section of this paper will examine the specific implications for the designer by suggesting ways in which these recent developments can be used to assist architects..." (p. 2)

Section titles like "How Might These Strands be Integrated?" (p. 11) and "Implications for Architectural Design" (p. 16) indicate synthesis and application of existing knowledge rather than new empirical data.
The "Conclusions" reiterate that it's a "tentative set of ideas" and a "springboard for future collaborative efforts." (p. 17)
title: Navigating Complex Buildings: Cognition, Neuroscience and Architectural Design
authors: R.C. Dalton, C. Hölscher and H.J. Spiers, 2015

findings.antecedent: Complex built space navigation
findings.consequent: Activity in a diverse network of brain regions (hippocampus, parahippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, posterior parietal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex)
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: it is evident that a diverse network of brain regions are engaged during the navigation of complex built space.

findings.antecedent: Hippocampus
findings.consequent: Storing an allocentric cognitive map for navigation
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: Evidence suggests the hippocampus is responsible for storing an allocentric cognitive map of the environment to guide navigation.

findings.antecedent: Parahippocampus
findings.consequent: Processing topographical information, determining current location, storing perceived environment information
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: The parahippocampus may be important for processing topographical information necessary to determine current location and store information about the perceived environment.

findings.antecedent: Retrosplenial cortex
findings.consequent: Translating allocentric map information into egocentric information
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: Retrosplenial cortex is thought to help translate the allocentric map information into egocentric information...

findings.antecedent: Posterior parietal cortex
findings.consequent: Processing egocentric information to guide bodily movement or imagine movement during planning
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: ...which is processed in posterior parietal cortex to guide bodily movement or imagine movement during planning.

findings.antecedent: Medial prefrontal cortex
findings.consequent: Planning routes, monitoring possible options, keeping goal in mind during navigation
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: The prefrontal cortex is important for planning routes, monitoring possible options and keeping the goal in mind during navigation.

findings.antecedent: Place cells (in hippocampus)
findings.consequent: Firing action potentials when an animal is in a particular location (place field)
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 5)
findings.quote: These exist in the hippocampus proper and fire action potentials (sending electrical signals to other cells) when an animal is in a particular location in the environment...

findings.antecedent: Place cells
findings.consequent: Response to changes in boundaries, distant landmarks, large-scale sensory aspects (floor/wall colors)
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 6)
findings.quote: They respond predominately to changes in the boundaries, distant landmarks, and large-scale sensory aspects of the environment, such as the floor and wall colors.

findings.antecedent: Head-direction cells (in presubiculum, anterior thalamus, retrosplenial cortex)
findings.consequent: Activity tuned to certain head-directions (internal compass)
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 6)
findings.quote: Instead, these cells offer something akin to an internal compass by expressing activity tuned to certain head-directions in the current environment.

findings.antecedent: Grid cells (in medial entorhinal cortex, subiculum)
findings.consequent: Multiple place fields arranged in a tessellating grid-like pattern
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 6)
findings.quote: Grid cell generate multiple place fields arranged in a tessellating grid-like pattern across the environment.

findings.antecedent: Grid cells
findings.consequent: Inputs to place cells about distance travelled
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 6)
findings.quote: It is thought that grid cells provide inputs to place cells about the distance travelled in the environment.

findings.antecedent: Boundary vector cells (in subiculum)
findings.consequent: Signaling location of borders in an environment
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 6)
findings.quote: Boundary vector cells [20] are also thought to provide inputs about the environment, and as their name suggests, they signal the location of borders in a given environment.

findings.antecedent: Egocentric spatial representations (in posterior parietal cortex)
findings.consequent: Coding information relative to the body (hand, torso, head, eye)
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 7)
findings.quote: Rather than mapping space relative to the environment, many of these cells code information relative to the body, forming egocentric spatial representations.

findings.antecedent: Integration of egocentric and allocentric spatial information
findings.consequent: Creation of an internal map of an environment and navigation
findings.source: What Does the Brain Do During the Navigation of Complex Built Space and How Does It Map It? (p. 7)
findings.quote: In order to create an internal map of an environment and navigate it, egocentric spatial information must be integrated with allocentric information...

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (visual access, architectural differentiation, layout complexity, signs/maps)
findings.consequent: Guiding human wayfinding behavior and spatial learning
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 8)
findings.quote: Authors like Weisman [27] have provided taxonomic views of how perceptual features of the built environment (both indoor and outdoor) guide human wayfinding behavior and spatial learning.

findings.antecedent: Spatial knowledge acquisition
findings.consequent: Progression from landmark knowledge to route knowledge to survey knowledge (most sophisticated)
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 8)
findings.quote: This progression, from least to most complex (landmark to route to survey knowledge) is also the order in which spatial knowledge is often thought to be acquired [28].

findings.antecedent: Salience of landmarks, individual differences, wayfinding task
findings.consequent: Role in people's selection, use, and recall of landmarks
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 8)
findings.quote: For example, there is evidence that landmarks do appear play a role during navigation, although these are less generalizable or universally applicable... salience of landmarks, individual differences and the particular form of wayfinding task all appear to play a role in people's selection, use and recall of landmarks [30, 31].

findings.antecedent: Routes with fewer turns
findings.consequent: Perceived/recalled as metrically shorter
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 9)
findings.quote: Routes with fewer turns are perceived of, or recalled, as being metrically shorter than those containing more changes in direction [32, 33].

findings.antecedent: Slight misalignments of spatial elements (rooms, corridors)
findings.consequent: Canonicalised to cardinal angles (e.g., 90° angle recalled as right-angle)
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 9)
findings.quote: Slight misalignments of spatial elements, for example rooms or corridors, are often canonicalised to cardinal angles.

findings.antecedent: Multi-level environments (subsequent floors)
findings.consequent: Assumption that subsequent floors will tend to resemble preceding floors in spatial layout
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 9)
findings.quote: Hölscher et al. [25] discovered an overriding assumption that subsequent floors will tend to resemble preceding floors, in terms of spatial layout and general spatial structure.

findings.antecedent: Defeated assumptions about floor resemblance in multi-level environments
findings.consequent: Measurable effect on wayfinding performance
findings.source: What can Cognitive Studies Tell us About Navigation in Complex Buildings? (p. 9)
findings.quote: When such assumptions are defeated, the resultant effect of wayfinding performance is measurable.

findings.antecedent: Space integration (measured mathematically as accessibility)
findings.consequent: Aggregate flows of people through specific spaces
findings.source: What Does Space Syntax Measure About Structures of Space and What Does it Tell us? (p. 10)
findings.quote: In essence, the more 'integrated' the space (on average, how accessible a space is from all other spaces, measured mathematically) the more people are likely to pass through it.

findings.antecedent: Angular-based space syntax measures (least angle)
findings.consequent: Correlation with observed pedestrian movement flows
findings.source: Table 1 (p. 10) and section (p. 9)
findings.quote: Mean Values across Neighbourhoods: Least angle Combined (0.649)

findings.antecedent: Intelligible environment (local spatial variables relate to global spatial properties)
findings.consequent: Ability to find way around complex building/environment, ability to draw inferences about one from the other
findings.source: What Does Space Syntax Measure About Structures of Space and What Does it Tell us? (p. 9)
findings.quote: Intelligibility is another concept from Hillier [34] that suggests that our ability to find our way around a complex building or environment is partly dependent upon the relationship between local spatial variables and global spatial properties...

findings.antecedent: Well-connected spaces in an intelligible environment
findings.consequent: Tendency to be highly strategic spaces within larger spatial structure, acting as visual cues for wayfinding
findings.source: What Does Space Syntax Measure About Structures of Space and What Does it Tell us? (p. 9)
findings.quote: In an intelligible environment, suggests Hillier, spaces that are well connected will also tend to be highly strategic spaces within their larger spatial structure. These connections act as visual cues for the wayfinding pedestrian...

findings.antecedent: Rat subjects exploring a helical stair-like environment
findings.consequent: Radically different patterns of grid cell firing in the third dimension (columnar-packing) compared to horizontal space
findings.source: Multi-level Environments (p. 13)
findings.quote: it was discovered that rat subjects, exploring a helical stair-like environment, produced radically different patterns of firing in the third dimension, i.e. it appears that the hippocampus encodes space differently in vertical and horizontal space.

findings.antecedent: Building users encountering multi-story buildings that radically depart from the model of floor resemblance
findings.consequent: Rapid disorientation
findings.source: Multi-level Environments (p. 13)
findings.quote: ...when a building is encountered that radically departs from this model (i.e. Subsequent floors do not resemble lower floors in terms of general layout and arrangement, see Fig. 5 for an example of such an environment) then subjects can become rapidly disorientated.

findings.antecedent: Hebbian synapse firing (cells firing simultaneously)
findings.consequent: Strengthening of interconnections between cells, formation of synaptic chains (e.g., sequence of place cells along a route)
findings.source: Intelligibility (p. 14)
findings.quote: One possible way of linking these different properties would be through a process of Hebbian synapse firing (in which any pair of cells that happen to fire simultaneously will evolve to strengthen their interconnections.

findings.antecedent: Straighter, more direct routes (fewer changes of direction)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 16)
findings.quote: Straighter, more direct, routes are significantly preferable to routes containing many changes of direction.

findings.antecedent: Breaking up long corridors to create 'places' (aesthetically)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 16)
findings.quote: This may work aesthetically at a local level but will certainly hinder wayfinding [47].

findings.antecedent: Unimpeded lines of sight connecting entrance spaces, key central spaces (atria) to vertical circulation (stairs, lifts, escalators)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding, comprehensibility
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 16)
findings.quote: Ensure unimpeded lines of sight connecting entrance spaces and other key, central spaces such as atria to the means of vertical circulation: stairs, lifts and escalators. These sight lines are crucial...

findings.antecedent: Shallower angles of turning (closer to straight-on, avoiding >90° turns)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding, orientation
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Where changes of direction/orientation are unavoidable, shallower angles of turning (closer to straight-on) are preferable to sharp turns (and in particular try to avoid turning angles greater than 90°; forcing a building user to turn back can be disorienting).

findings.antecedent: Differences in layout between floors
findings.consequent: Undue confusion for building users
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Wherever possible ensure that differences in layout between floors are not too great. Building users will assume that each floor is laid out in an analogous manner to the preceding floors. Deviating from this too greatly will cause undue confusion [25].

findings.antecedent: Frequent and regular sightlines to external views, atria, or visually prominent architectural features (invariant visual information)
findings.consequent: Orientation checks in buildings
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: In a building, equivalent invariant information can be provided by ensuring frequent and regular sightlines to features such as external views, atria, or visually prominent architectural features.

findings.antecedent: Atria
findings.consequent: 'Short-cut' to survey-knowledge (top-down and global knowledge), facilitating views to other floors
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Atria can serve another useful purpose: they can provide a ‘short-cut' to survey-knowledge (or top-down and global as opposed to eye-level and local), as they facilitate views to and hence knowledge of other floors that would otherwise be unavailable.

findings.antecedent: Excessive complexity in design
findings.consequent: Conflict with wayfinding functional requirements
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Excessive complexity should be avoided. Again, here lies potential for conflict between architectural intent and wayfinding functional requirements.

findings.antecedent: Strong visual similarity between locations at a local level (e.g., symmetrical layouts, identical corridors)
findings.consequent: Building users becoming lost or disorientated
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Building users may become lost or disorientated in locations that bear strong visual similarity, at a local level, to other locations in the same building (this can often occur in strongly symmetrical layouts, i.e. one corridor is identical to a neighboring, parallel corridor) [27].

findings.antecedent: Deliberate utilization of architectural features as 'landmarks' (placed at decision points, large visibility-catchment area)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding
findings.source: Design Heuristics for Architects (p. 17)
findings.quote: Another method is to deliberately utilize architectural features as ‘landmarks'. These work best if placed at decision points and if they are have a large visibility-catchment area, and so can be seen from multiple locations [30, 31].

limitations: The paper presents a "tentative set of ideas" and serves as a "springboard for future collaborative efforts," indicating it is not a definitive statement but a starting point for research. (p. 1, p. 17)
There is a significant "gulf" in scale between the different academic fields (from society to a single neuron) that needs to be bridged for effective integration. (p. 11)
Design recommendations, such as favoring "straighter, more direct routes," can conflict with aesthetic requirements, potentially hindering wayfinding if aesthetics are prioritized. (p. 16)
Relying on internal décor (e.g., prominent use of color) as a navigational cue is problematic because it can be unwittingly altered over the building's lifetime. (p. 17)

The interpretation of grid cell findings in humans, particularly regarding 2.5-dimensional perception of space, relies on the assumption that "grid cells in human brains are sufficiently similar to rat brains." (p. 13)
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for integrating neuroscience, spatial cognition, and space syntax research to inform architectural design for user-friendly buildings. It synthesizes current knowledge on brain mechanisms for navigation (e.g., place, grid, head-direction cells), cognitive processes of spatial knowledge acquisition (landmark, route, survey), and space syntax measures (integration, angularity, intelligibility). Key findings include the brain's differential encoding of vertical and horizontal space, the impact of layout complexity and floor similarity on wayfinding, and the predictive power of angular-based space syntax measures for pedestrian movement. The paper concludes with design heuristics for architects, such as favoring straighter routes, ensuring clear sightlines to vertical circulation, maintaining floor layout consistency, and strategically placing architectural landmarks. Limitations include the challenge of bridging different scales of analysis and potential conflicts between wayfinding heuristics and aesthetic design goals.
